title: Thinking Tasks: Analysis, Planning and Decisions

thumbnail.headline: Show Me Your Reasoning
thumbnail.image: Navy background, a comparison table of three options with an assumptions list beside it and one assumption highlighted in amber, headline in teal Inter Bold.

slide.title: Show Me Your Reasoning
slide.body: A three-column comparison table (A, B, C) with a short 'Assumptions' list beside it; the weakest assumption highlighted in amber. Small tag: Prompt Engineering Masterclass · Lesson 8.

production_notes: [VERIFY] The claim that asking for step-by-step reasoning improves results varies between models. The voiceover says only that it 'often helps' and 'does not guarantee a correct answer'; do not change this wording to a stronger claim.
[VERSION] Free-tier availability of Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini must be checked before recording (content.md Review Flags).
Ravi, his café in Chennai and delivery partners A, B and C are hypothetical. Do not show real delivery-company names, uniforms or logos in stock footage.
Before/after prompts appear on code slides with the exact text from content.md, including [FEES AND TERMS] and [AMOUNT]; the voiceover summarises them.

Hook.voiceover: Which option should I choose? AI tools are happy to answer that question, often with great confidence. But a confident answer is only as good as the reasoning and the information behind it. Today, you will learn how to see that reasoning.
Hook.on_screen_text: Confident is not the same as right

Explain.voiceover: So far, you have used AI for writing, where you mostly check the wording. For thinking tasks, such as analysis, planning and decisions, you need to see the reasoning. Four prompt techniques often help.

Technique one: ask it to work step by step before it gives a recommendation. This makes the reasoning visible, so you can check each step. With many tools this often helps, but it does not guarantee a correct answer. Technique two: ask it to list the assumptions it is making. Seeing them lets you correct the wrong ones.

slide.title: Techniques 1 and 2
slide.body: 1. 'Work through this step by step before you recommend.' (often helps, no guarantee) 2. 'List the assumptions you are making.'

Explain.voiceover: Technique three: name the criteria. Instead of asking which is best, ask the tool to compare the options on cost, reliability and ease of use, in a table. Your criteria reflect your priorities, which the tool cannot know. Technique four: ask it to ask you up to five questions before it answers. This is useful when you are not sure what context matters.

slide.title: Techniques 3 and 4
slide.body: 3. Name the criteria: cost · reliability · ease of use, in a table. 4. 'Before you answer, ask me up to five questions.'

Explain.voiceover: After the analysis, one more request is very useful. Ask: what is the weakest assumption in your analysis? This asks the tool to question its own answer, and it often shows where you need to check facts yourself. It takes only one line to ask.

slide.title: The follow-up question
slide.body: "What is the weakest assumption in your analysis?"

Explain.voiceover: Think of a well-read friend helping you compare three flats to rent. They can organise your thinking, and point out things you forgot. But they have not visited the flats. So you still check the facts before you sign. The tool does not know current prices, local conditions or your finances unless you tell it.
Explain.stock_query: friends comparing apartment listings on laptop

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's try it. Ravi runs a small café in Chennai. He wants to start delivery, and he is comparing three delivery partners. He has their offers written down. He wants a clear comparison, not a general list.

His first prompt asks: which delivery partner is best for my café? The answer is a general list of things to consider, with no clear recommendation. It is polite and sensible, but it does not help him choose.

slide.title: Before
slide.body: Which delivery partner is best for my café?  → Output note in red: general checklist, no recommendation.

Demonstrate.voiceover: His second prompt describes the café: delivery within five kilometres, about thirty orders a day, mostly at lunch. It names three criteria: cost per order, lunchtime delivery time, and control over customer service. It includes each partner's terms. Then it asks the tool to work step by step, list its assumptions, show a table, and give a two-sentence recommendation.

slide.title: After
slide.body: Show the full 'After' prompt from content.md, with the three criteria and the last three lines (step by step, assumptions, table, two-sentence recommendation) highlighted.

Demonstrate.voiceover: The tool lists its assumptions. One is an average order value, and Ravi corrects it with his real figure. Then he asks for the weakest assumption. The tool says it had no information about lunchtime delivery times, and simply assumed they were equal for all three.

slide.title: Checking the assumptions
slide.body: Assumptions list: 'average order value about [AMOUNT]' (crossed out, corrected by Ravi) · 'lunchtime delivery times similar for all three' (amber, labelled 'weakest assumption').

Demonstrate.voiceover: So Ravi decides to test all three partners for one week before he chooses. The AI did not make the decision. It organised the information, and showed Ravi what he still needed to find out.
Demonstrate.stock_query: food delivery rider collecting order cafe

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to ask what should I do, and follow the recommendation without reading the reasoning. A recommendation can sound certain, even when it rests on a guessed number. Read the assumptions, correct the wrong ones, and ask for the weakest one before you act.

slide.title: Before you act
slide.body: Three steps: Read the assumptions → Correct the wrong ones → Ask for the weakest one.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, for thinking tasks, ask the tool to work step by step, list its assumptions, and compare options on criteria you name. Second, asking for the weakest assumption often shows what you need to check. Third, step-by-step prompts often help, but they do not guarantee a correct answer. The decision and the fact-checking stay with you.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Step by step · assumptions · your criteria. 2. Ask for the weakest assumption. 3. Often helps, never a guarantee: you decide and check.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will use a step-by-step prompt to compare two or three options for a real decision at work. Then you will ask the AI for the weakest assumption in its own analysis. It takes about twenty-five minutes. In the next lesson, we look at roles and multi-turn conversations. See you there.
